reasoning.Student A: The mechanism is strategy-proof, so truthful reporting of my preferences is a dominant strategy: no ranking I submit can give me a strictly better outcome than ranking schools in my true order, regardless of what others do. My true preferences are w > x > y > z. Even though many applicants favor y and I also have top priority at both w and y (w:1, y:1), I value w most—so I should list w first. Attempting to misrepresent (for example, listing y above w to hedge against competition) cannot improve my outcome under a strategy-proof mechanism. Therefore I will report my true ranking.
reasoning.Student B: Because the mechanism is strategy-proof, I cannot obtain a better outcome by misrepresenting my preferences regardless of what others do. My true ordering is x > w > y > z, so I should report that. Even though many applicants prefer y > x > w > z and my priorities are w:2, x:1, y:2, z:1, those facts do not create an incentive to lie under a strategy-proof mechanism. Ranking truthfully (x first, w second, y third, z last) is a dominant strategy.
reasoning.Student C: The mechanism is strategy-proof, so my dominant strategy is to report my true preferences; I cannot get a better outcome by misrepresenting my ranking regardless of what others do. My true ordering is w > x > y > z. Although many applicants favor y > x > w > z and my priority at y (4) is lower than at w and x (3), this does not change that truthful reporting is optimal under a strategy-proof mechanism. Therefore I will rank the schools in my true preference order.

Therefore I should (and should simply) report my true ranking.
